explainBack.prompt: Why can drawing a rough sketch or commenting on one region produce a better result than writing an ever-longer text prompt?
explainBack.response: Because words describe spatial arrangement ambiguously, while a sketch delivers the layout directly as visual context — the system receives where things go rather than a paragraph it must interpret. A comment narrows the editing target to one region, so the system changes less and preserves the rest. The output is still a freshly generated image, not an editable layered file, so precise text, measurements and brand details must be verified outside it.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (visual communication versus long prompts), P006 (rough map, smaller editing target, regeneration limit), P010 (use the richer context route).
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this answer in ordinary language; the causal chain from richer input context to more steerable output is explicit and honest about its limits.

unseenTransfer.prompt: Using this article's mechanism, how should the planner guide the tool, and what must they still not trust the image for?
unseenTransfer.response: They should sketch the room's rough layout first — stage here, dance floor there, table clusters at these positions — so the system gets a spatial map instead of an ambiguous paragraph, then use a comment pinned to one region ('swap this table cluster for a buffet line, keep everything else') for each single targeted edit. Because the tool regenerates an image rather than editing a data file, they must not trust it for real measurements, aisle clearances, fire-capacity numbers or exact signage text; those come from the venue's floor plan and regulations.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P006 (map and target mechanism, regeneration limit), P008 (one targeted edit at a time), P007 (measurements and factual details checked outside the picture).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The transfer succeeds: the article's context-routing mechanism resolves a genuinely new situation absent from the text and correctly predicts what the image cannot be trusted for.

incidentExplained.observation: What was released, when, what it adds and what it is not (a new general chat model) are all clear in sequence.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5 on September 8. It is the image-making and image-editing part of ChatGPT—not a new general chat model. The release adds ways to begin with a rough drawing or a template, place a comment on part of an image you want changed, and share the prompt behind an image.

OpenAI says Images 2.5 is rolling out across all ChatGPT tiers on desktop, mobile and web, as well as ChatGPT Work and Codex. The release notes add two important limits: templates are not yet available in Work mode, and existing image-generation limits have not changed. Because this is a rollout, a feature may not appear in every account at the same moment.

termsExplainedInContext.observation: Sketch, comment, template and rollout gain plain meaning at first use; 'context' is explained through the picture-versus-prompt contrast.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5 on September 8. It is the image-making and image-editing part of ChatGPT—not a new general chat model. The release adds ways to begin with a rough drawing or a template, place a comment on part of an image you want changed, and share the prompt behind an image.

A sketch gives the system a rough map: put the sofa here, leave space for a headline there, or make the product the largest object. A comment gives it a smaller editing target: change this sleeve, remove that lamp, keep the rest. The AI still generates a new image; it is not turning the result into a fully editable design file with independent text boxes and layers.

The larger lesson is current AI practice: when the product gives you a better way to provide context—a picture, a file, a marked region or a shared project—use that route instead of forcing the whole job into a longer prompt.

readerConsequenceSpecific.observation: Consequences land in specific reader situations: marketing asset drafting, room planning, and what still needs external checking.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: That distinction matters for real work. A marketing manager could sketch the arrangement of a social post, then ask for visual directions before a designer builds the final asset. Someone planning a room could draw the furniture placement instead of writing a paragraph about left, right and centre. But exact copy, measurements, brand rules and important factual details still need checking outside the finished picture.

If the new tools appear in your account, try them on a task where layout matters. Draw the rough arrangement first, add the few details that must be preserved, and make one targeted edit at a time. That tests the real improvement: whether you can steer the image without rebuilding the whole idea after every change.
